actions.justification: Mandatory first step — confirm and document hemodynamic instability (HR 138, BP 76/44, SpO2 78%, RR 32) to establish severity and guide management of suspected massive PE.
Mandatory — calculate Wells score to stratify PE probability. This patient has high pre-test probability given recent THR, immobilization, tachycardia, and clinical presentation consistent with PE.
SpO2 of 78% is critically low and immediately life-threatening. Supplemental oxygen must be initiated urgently to correct hypoxemia while diagnostic workup proceeds.

Mandatory action per guidelines for PE workup. D-dimer ordered as part of initial diagnostic assessment, though with this high-probability presentation (post-THR, immobilization, hemodynamic instability, SpO2 78%), clinical suspicion is already extremely high.

ECG is indicated in suspected massive PE to assess for right heart strain patterns (S1Q3T3, new RBBB, sinus tachycardia) and to rule out alternative diagnoses such as MI or arrhythmia contributing to hemodynamic collapse.

Urgent bedside echocardiogram is critical to confirm right ventricular dilation/strain consistent with massive PE, assess hemodynamics, and support decision-making for thrombolysis per ESC PE guidelines in this patient with shock (MAP 55, BP 76/44, HR 138, SpO2 78%).

CT pulmonary angiography is the gold standard to confirm massive PE before thrombolysis. Patient has high clinical probability (Wells score, recent hip replacement, immobilization) with hemodynamic collapse. Confirmation needed before systemic thrombolysis.
Patient has cardiogenic shock with MAP 55 mmHg and BP 76/44. Vasopressor support (norepinephrine) is required to maintain perfusion pressure while definitive PE treatment (thrombolysis) is prepared.

Cautious IV fluid resuscitation indicated for hemodynamic support in massive PE with shock. Note: aggressive fluids are avoided in RV failure, but modest fluid challenge can help support preload in distributive component of shock.
ECG (via available imaging action) can reveal right heart strain patterns (S1Q3T3, new RBBB, sinus tachycardia) consistent with massive PE, supporting diagnosis and guiding urgency of thrombolysis.

Bedside echocardiogram is critical in this hemodynamically unstable patient with suspected massive PE to assess RV dilation, septal shift, and RV dysfunction — confirming high-risk PE and supporting decision to proceed with thrombolysis per ESC guidelines.

This patient has massive/high-risk PE with obstructive shock (BP 76/44, MAP 55, HR 138, SpO2 78%, altered mental status) following recent hip replacement. ESC guidelines strongly recommend systemic thrombolysis for massive PE with hemodynamic instability. Anticoagulation alone carries unacceptably high mortality (25-65%) in this setting. The guideline explicitly forbids delaying thrombolysis in massive PE.
